rawText: In the Fall of 1923, the family’s loyalty and cooperation were rewarded with a brand new 1923 Model T Ford automobile. Even though it was a standard size car of that day, it had to have been built of special steel, since the entire family of 13 children would be packed into the car on Sunday afternoons with Mama in the front seat holding baby Claude, Calvin in the middle peeping over the dash board, and Papa in the driver’s seat. This mode of travel meant good-bye to traveling to church on Sunday and grocery shopping in town in a wagon drawn by a team of mules. With this euphoria of progress, tragedy had to come. It did in the form of the sudden death of our youngest brother of five months, Jeremiah Douglas, a victim of an untimely accident. This being the first death within the family, the grief that it brought served to remind the family that we also are merely children of destiny. The progress of these two parents became even more obvious over the next three years when in 1926, a new Model T Ford truck was added in order to give greater mobility to the farming operation. With the purchase of an additional tract of farm land in 1927, the family finally entered the industrial farming era. This necessitated the purchase of the first farm tractor and implements. This brought the family to another pressing need, the accommodation for the growth and development of 13 children. Within the midst of a great depression in 1928, our parents ventured out to build a new home: a modern 9-room, 2 story structure with the convenience very much up-to-date in those days. With the help of the older brothers and three carpenters and a mason, our family home was completed during the Fall of 1928. Even though our home was built before Rural Electrification became available, our home was equipped with modern gas lights, a bathroom and basement. This self-help achievement was rewarded by the purchase of a Ford roadster car for the boys, and later a new Chevrolet Sedan car for the family. The next major concern of our parents was the education of their children. There being no available high school for students of our race within the immediate vicinity, the older sons were sent off to high school at Weldon and later to Henderson Institute. When the Eastman High School at Ringwood, N.C. extended its patronage area to include our community, our parents were financially instrumental in securing the first school bus which made it possible for the children to secure a high school education. As a result, three of the children went on to college. The religious education was not overlooked. The family rule was "religious commitment must precede all other commitments whether they be economic, political, or social". The commitment to Christ, joining the church, and attending Sunday School were top priorities. The boys weren't allowed to use the car, and the girls weren't allowed to entertain their boyfriends until after they had attended church services and Sunday School. Even though the children were taught the importance of discipline and thrift, they were also reminded that the church and other worthy institutions serving those who aren't so fortunate should undergird all our efforts toward financial achievement. As the years passed, and while some of the children grew into adulthood and some married, World War II came along. six of the men of the family had to answer the draft, five of whom served overseas, two served in the combat zone in the Army. Grady and Wilbert served in the Navy, while Claude, Calvin, and Jesse served in the Army. Other brothers served in critical defense industries on the homefront.
